blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Say a temperature sensor logs a reading every single hour, all day, every day, for a month. That is a lot of rows, and most of the time you do not actually care about every single hour. You care about the daily average, or maybe the weekly high. Somebody eventually asks you: what was the average temperature each day? You already know exactly how to answer a question shaped like that, because you just spent the Data Manipulation module learning groupby(), and this is a groupby question wearing a disguise.

resample() is pandas name for exactly that disguise removed. It is groupby, applied specifically to time based data. Instead of splitting your data by the distinct values in a column, like region or category, resample splits your data into buckets of time, every hour, every day, every week, whatever grain you choose, and then applies an aggregation to each bucket, then combines the results back into a single Series or DataFrame. Same three steps you already know. Same mental model. The only thing that changed is what you are grouping by.

items: A bank statement that shows one line per month instead of one line per transaction.
A fitness tracker rolling up every step you took in a day into a single daily step count.
A weather app showing you today's high and low instead of every temperature reading it recorded.
A quarterly earnings report built by rolling up daily sales into three month totals.

blocks.text: Every one of those is a resample question wearing a different outfit. And because you already understand split, apply, combine cold from the groupby lesson, the fastest way to learn resample is to map it directly onto what you already know, not to learn it as some brand new, unrelated pandas feature.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame splitting one way by a region column into groupby style groups, and another way by a time slice into resample style daily buckets
blocks.caption: Same DataFrame, two different grouping keys: a column value, or a slice of time.

blocks.text: This lesson covers two directions you can resample in. Downsampling means going from a finer grain to a coarser one, like hourly readings rolled up into daily averages. Upsampling is the exact opposite, going from a coarser grain to a finer one, like monthly totals broken out into daily values. Both directions start with the exact same resample() call, but they behave very differently once you get there, and that difference is most of what this lesson is about.
2. Resample Is GroupBy for Time

Remember the three steps from the groupby lesson. Split breaks your DataFrame into smaller pieces, one piece per group. Apply runs a function on each of those pieces independently. Combine glues the individual answers back into one final result. resample runs through the exact same three steps, with one change: the thing that decides which rows belong together is no longer a column's distinct values, it is a slice of time.
2.1 The Same Split-Apply-Combine, a Different Grouping Key

Line the two up side by side and the parallel is exact. groupby splits your rows by whatever distinct values live in a column. resample splits your rows by whatever time bucket their timestamp falls into. Everything downstream of that first split, applying a function, combining the answers, works identically either way.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","groupby(\"region\")","resample(\"D\")"],"rows":[["Split","One group per distinct region value","One group per calendar day"],["Apply","mean computed within each region","mean computed within each day"],["Combine","One row per region in the result","One row per day in the result"]]}

blocks.text: Syntactically resample looks almost identical to groupby too. You call .resample() on your DataFrame or Series, pass it a frequency string instead of a column name, then chain an aggregation onto it, exactly the way you would chain .mean() or .sum() onto a groupby object.

code.content:
# groupby: group by a column's distinct values
orders.groupby("region")["total"].mean()

# resample: group by a slice of time
readings.resample("D")["reading"].mean()

blocks.text: 2.2 Why Resample Needs a DatetimeIndex

There is one requirement resample has that groupby never did. groupby is happy to group by any column you hand it. resample needs to know how to carve up time, and it does that by reading your DataFrame's index. Specifically, your index has to be a DatetimeIndex, the same index type built by pd.date_range() and produced automatically whenever you parse a column of dates with pd.to_datetime() and set it as the index.

code.content:
df = df.set_index("timestamp")
df.index
# DatetimeIndex(['2024-06-01 06:00:00', '2024-06-01 07:00:00', ...],
#                dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)

df.resample("D").mean()

blocks.title: Resample without a DatetimeIndex fails
blocks.content: Call resample on a DataFrame that still has a plain integer index, or a date sitting in an ordinary column instead of the index, and pandas raises a TypeError telling you it only understands DatetimeIndex, PeriodIndex, or TimedeltaIndex. Set your date column as the index first with set_index, or read it in with a parse_dates and index_col argument, before you ever call resample.

blocks.text: This is also exactly where the frequency codes from the date_range lesson come back. resample takes the same D, h, W, M, and similar frequency strings you used to build a range of dates in the first place, because resample is really just using date_range internally to decide where the bucket boundaries fall.
3. Downsampling: Fewer, Bigger Buckets

Downsampling means going from a finer time grain to a coarser one. Hourly readings become daily averages. Daily totals become weekly totals. Weekly numbers become monthly numbers. You are always moving from more rows to fewer rows, because you are merging several old buckets into one new, wider bucket. This is the direction of resample that behaves the most like an ordinary groupby, since every new bucket is built entirely out of rows that already existed in your data.

blocks.alt: Hourly readings splitting into two daily buckets, one for each calendar day, each bucket then reduced to a single daily average
blocks.caption: Downsampling merges many existing rows into fewer, wider buckets.

blocks.text: 3.1 The Frequency Codes You Already Know

Every frequency code you learned building ranges of dates works exactly the same way inside resample. D still means calendar day, W still means week, h still means hour. The only difference is what that code is being used for. In date_range it decided the spacing between the dates you generated. In resample it decides the width of each bucket your existing data gets grouped into.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Code","Bucket width","Typical use"],"rows":[["h","One hour","Sensor or server metrics logged frequently"],["D","One calendar day","Daily totals or daily averages"],["W","One week, ending on Sunday by default","Weekly sales or weekly summaries"],["M","One calendar month, labeled by month end","Monthly revenue or monthly reports"],["Q","One quarter","Quarterly business reporting"]]}

blocks.text: You can also scale any of these with a leading number, the same way you could in date_range. "3h" buckets every three hours together. "2W" buckets every two weeks together. The rule does not change just because you are aggregating existing data instead of generating new dates.

code.content:
readings.resample("3h").mean()   # bucket every 3 hours together
readings.resample("2D").sum()    # bucket every 2 days together

blocks.text: 3.2 Worked Example: Hourly Readings to Daily Averages
Forty eight hourly sensor readings, spanning two full days, indexed by a DatetimeIndex built with an hourly frequency.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)
hourly = pd.DataFrame(
    {"reading": np.random.uniform(60, 85, size=48).round(1)},
    index=pd.date_range("2024-06-01", periods=48, freq="h"),
)
hourly.head()

#                      reading
# 2024-06-01 00:00:00     73.7
# 2024-06-01 01:00:00     77.9
# 2024-06-01 02:00:00     75.1
# 2024-06-01 03:00:00     73.6
# 2024-06-01 04:00:00     70.6

blocks.text: Now roll those 48 hourly rows up into one average per calendar day.

Walk that through split, apply, combine and it stops feeling like magic. Split groups the 48 hourly rows into 2 buckets, one for June 1st and one for June 2nd, purely based on which calendar day each timestamp falls inside. Apply runs mean on each of those two buckets independently, 24 numbers going in, 1 number coming out, twice. Combine stitches those two daily averages into the two row result above, with each bucket's date as the new index.

blocks.alt: 48 hourly rows flowing through resample D into two results, a June 1 mean of 75.26 and a June 2 mean of 72.05
blocks.caption: The exact same three steps you know from groupby, applied to hourly sensor data.

blocks.title: Other aggregations work exactly the same way
blocks.content: mean is not special here. resample("D").sum() gives you a daily total instead of a daily average, resample("D").max() gives you the daily high, resample("D").count() tells you how many readings landed in each day. Anything you could chain onto a groupby object, you can chain onto a resample object too.

blocks.text: 4. Upsampling: More, Smaller Buckets

Upsampling is the opposite move. You go from a coarser grain to a finer one, monthly numbers broken out into daily values, daily numbers broken out into hourly values. The call looks identical, you still write resample and pass a frequency code, but this time that frequency code is finer than your original data, not coarser.

This is where resample stops behaving like a normal groupby and starts doing something groupby never had to do. Downsampling only ever merges rows that already exist, there was never a risk of anything missing. Upsampling has to invent new rows that were never in your original data at all, because you are asking for more timestamps than you started with.

blocks.alt: One monthly total for January splitting into 31 daily rows, February into 29 daily rows, and March into 31 daily rows after upsampling
blocks.caption: Upsampling produces far more rows than you started with, one for every point on the finer calendar.

blocks.text: 4.1 New Rows Start Out Empty

Say you have one row of revenue per month, for three months. Upsample that to daily and pandas needs to produce roughly ninety rows, one for every single day across those three months. Only three of those ninety rows had a real number behind them a moment ago. The other eighty seven did not exist in your data at all.

blocks.title: Upsampling creates NaN, it does not invent data
blocks.content: asfreq() is the honest, do nothing version of upsampling. It builds every new timestamp the finer frequency requires and leaves each brand new row as NaN, because pandas genuinely has no idea what belongs there. If you stop here and forget to fill those rows, every downstream calculation, a mean, a sum, a plot, will be quietly working with a Series that is now mostly empty.

blocks.alt: January 1 holding a real value, January 2 and January 3 shown as empty new rows, then February 1 holding the next real value
blocks.caption: Every row upsampling creates in between two real values starts out completely empty.

blocks.text: 4.2 Forward Fill: Carrying the Last Known Value Forward

The simplest fix is the same ffill you already met in the missing values lesson. Instead of leaving new rows as NaN, ffill carries the most recent real value forward into every empty row that follows it, until the next real value takes over.

That works well when the value genuinely does not change in between two known points, a monthly subscription price, a fixed interest rate, an inventory count that only updates once a month. It is a much worse fit for anything actually drifting steadily between two points, because ffill produces a stair step pattern, flat, then a sudden jump, flat again, when reality was probably smoother than that.

blocks.alt: January 1 value 12000 carried forward unchanged into January 2 and January 3, then a real value of 15500 taking over on February 1
blocks.caption: ffill repeats the last known value for every empty row, right up until the next real value arrives.

blocks.text: 4.3 Interpolate: Estimating the Values In Between

interpolate() is the more sophisticated cousin of ffill and bfill. Rather than repeating one of the two known values, it estimates a smooth path between them. Linear interpolation, the default, assumes a straight line between one known value and the next, and fills every point on that line for you.

Notice the difference from ffill. ffill would have kept every day in January flat at 12000, then jumped straight to 15500 on February 1st. interpolate instead climbs steadily across January, a little higher each day, so the transition between the two known months looks like a gradual trend rather than a sudden cliff.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","What it does","Best for"],"rows":[["ffill","Repeats the last known value until the next real one","Values that genuinely stay constant, like a price or a status"],["bfill","Repeats the next known value backward","Rare, mostly used when a lookahead is acceptable"],["interpolate","Estimates a smooth path between two known values","Values that drift gradually, like temperature or a trend line"]]}

blocks.alt: A known starting value connected through two smoothly estimated intermediate steps to a known ending value, forming a gradual path rather than a flat repeat
blocks.caption: interpolate lays down a gradual path between two known values instead of repeating one of them.

blocks.title: interpolate has options too
blocks.content: The default straight line interpolation is called linear, but interpolate also supports curved methods like polynomial and spline for data that clearly does not move in a straight line. For most everyday upsampling though, linear is the sensible starting point.

blocks.text: 5. The OHLC Pattern

There is one aggregation built specifically for resample that you will not find on a plain groupby call nearly as often: ohlc, short for open, high, low, close. It comes straight out of financial time series, where a candlestick chart for a stock needs exactly those four numbers for every single time bucket: the first price recorded, the highest price recorded, the lowest price recorded, and the last price recorded.

One call, one bucket, four numbers back, computed all at once instead of chaining first, max, min, and last separately. Notice that close does not have to differ from low, it just happens to land there in the first bucket above, because the lowest price recorded also happened to be the last one. You will see this constantly if you ever touch stock, crypto, or commodity data, since candlestick charts are the standard way that industry visualizes price movement. Even outside finance it is worth knowing ohlc exists, because that same first, max, min, last combination is occasionally exactly what you want for any bucketed value that swings around a lot, not only prices.

blocks.alt: One price bucket branching into four values computed at once: the open as the first price, the high as the max price, the low as the min price, and the close as the last price
blocks.caption: ohlc computes all four candlestick values from a single bucket in one call.

blocks.text: 6. Resample vs a Plain GroupBy on a Date Component

A fair question at this point: if resample really is just groupby with time as the key, why not extract the date yourself and group by that directly? Something like df.groupby(df.index.date).mean() looks like it should give you the same daily average as df.resample("D").mean(). Most of the time, on paper, it very nearly does. But there is one crucial difference, and it comes straight out of the gap revealing behavior you already saw in the date_range lesson.
6.1 GroupBy Only Ever Sees the Rows You Actually Have

groupby(df.index.date) works by looking at the distinct values actually present in your data and building one group per distinct value it finds. If your sensor happened to log zero readings on June 5th, June 5th simply never shows up as a distinct value, so groupby never builds a group for it, and the result skips straight from June 4th to June 6th without a trace.

code.content:
gappy = pd.Series(
    [74.1, 71.8, 69.9],
    index=pd.to_datetime(["2024-06-03", "2024-06-04", "2024-06-06"]),
)
gappy.groupby(gappy.index.date).mean()

# 2024-06-03    74.1
# 2024-06-04    71.8
# 2024-06-06    69.9      # June 5th is just gone, not zero, not NaN, gone

blocks.text: 6.2 Resample Knows the Full Calendar

resample builds its buckets from the frequency code first, the same way date_range builds a full, evenly spaced range of dates before anything else happens. It decides every bucket boundary that should exist between your data's start and end, June 3rd, June 4th, June 5th, June 6th, and only afterward goes looking for rows to drop into each one. A bucket with genuinely zero underlying rows still gets built, it just comes back as NaN instead of quietly vanishing.

code.content:
gappy.resample("D").mean()

# 2024-06-03    74.1
# 2024-06-04    71.8
# 2024-06-05     NaN     # resample knows this day should exist, and flags it
# 2024-06-06    69.9

blocks.title: This is the same gap revealing behavior from date_range
blocks.content: date_range never skips a date just because nothing happened to land on it, it always produces a complete, evenly spaced sequence. resample inherits that same property because it is built out of date_range internally. That is exactly why resample is the frequency aware, safer choice whenever a missing bucket is meaningful information you actually want to see, rather than a row you would rather not think about.

blocks.alt: A gap on June 5 with no data leading two paths, groupby on a date component that leaves June 5 missing entirely, versus resample D that shows June 5 as NaN
blocks.caption: The same gap treated two different ways: silently skipped, or explicitly flagged as missing.

blocks.content: {"headers":["","groupby(df.index.date)","resample(\"D\")"],"rows":[["Builds groups from","Distinct values present in the data","The full frequency, regardless of what is present"],["A day with zero rows","Silently missing from the result","Present in the result, showing NaN"],["Frequency aware","No","Yes"],["Good default for time series","Rarely","Almost always"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Transaction Data, Both Directions
Fourteen days of daily revenue for a small online store, two full weeks in a row.
From here you can move in either direction resample supports, and the exact same Series is the starting point for both.
7.1 Downsampling to Weekly Totals
Rolling this up to a weekly view is a one line downsample: coarser grain, fewer rows, sum since revenue is additive.

code.content:
weekly_totals = daily_totals.resample("W").sum()
weekly_totals

# 2024-06-09    3738
# 2024-06-16    3867
# Freq: W-SUN, Name: revenue, dtype: int64

blocks.text: Two weekly totals out of fourteen daily ones, each week labeled by the Sunday it ends on by default. Split grouped the fourteen days into two seven day buckets, apply summed each bucket, combine returned the two row result. Nothing new conceptually, this is the exact same downsample pattern from the sensor example earlier in this lesson, just with sum instead of mean and a coarser target frequency.

blocks.alt: Fourteen daily revenue totals flowing through resample W sum into two results, a week 1 total of 3738 and a week 2 total of 3867
blocks.caption: The same fourteen days rolled up into two weekly totals.

blocks.text: 7.2 Upsampling to Hourly with Interpolation

Now go the other direction on that same Series. Upsampling fourteen days down to an hourly grain means pandas has to build over three hundred new timestamps, and only fourteen of them, midnight on each of the original days, start out with a real number.

asfreq shows the honest, empty version first, on purpose, so the gap is impossible to miss. ffill would technically work here too, flat revenue for every hour until the next known day kicks in, but a store's revenue does not actually jump instantly at midnight and then sit perfectly flat for twenty four hours. interpolate is the better fit, since it treats revenue as drifting gradually between one day's total and the next.

Between June 3rd's 420 and June 4th's 388, interpolate lays down twenty three smoothly decreasing values, one per hour, closing the gap in equal steps rather than repeating 420 for a full day and then dropping straight to 388 at midnight. The same fourteen numbers you started with are all still exactly where they were, resample and interpolate together just filled in a believable, gradual path everywhere in between.

blocks.alt: The same fourteen daily totals flowing through resample h interpolate into a much longer hourly series, with smoothly filled values across June 3 and June 4
blocks.caption: The same fourteen days spread out into an hourly view, with every gap filled by a gradual path.

blocks.title: Pick the direction the question actually asks for
blocks.content: Downsampling and upsampling are not two different tools, they are one tool, resample, pointed in two different directions. The only real decision you have to make each time is whether the frequency you are resampling to is coarser than what you already have, which needs an aggregation like sum or mean, or finer, which needs a fill strategy like ffill or interpolate.

blocks.text: 8. Recap

items: resample() is groupby, specifically for time based data. Same split, apply, combine model, the grouping key is a slice of time instead of a column's distinct values.
It requires a DatetimeIndex, and it reuses the exact same frequency codes, D, h, W, M, and their scaled versions, that you used to build ranges of dates.
Downsampling moves from a finer grain to a coarser one, merging existing rows with an aggregation like mean or sum. No new rows get created.
Upsampling moves from a coarser grain to a finer one, and it creates brand new rows that start out completely empty. Those rows need an explicit fill strategy.
ffill carries the last known value forward. interpolate estimates a smooth path between two known values instead, the more sophisticated cousin of ffill and bfill from the missing values lesson.
ohlc computes open, high, low, and close for each bucket in one call, standard for financial time series, worth knowing about even outside finance.

resample beats a plain groupby on a manually extracted date component because it is frequency aware. A bucket with zero rows still shows up as NaN instead of disappearing, the same gap revealing behavior you saw in date_range.
